title: 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday: A Welcome Back Edition
author: Episcopal Academy CTL
summary: Episcopal Academy's Center for Teaching & Learning opens its weekly "What Do You Need? Wednesday" faculty newsletter for the new school year with a four-part digest that pairs practical support with intellectual framing for teachers returning to campus. The lead section reframes early faculty pushback against the school's new "Portrait of a Graduate" competency framework by citing UK educator Tom Sherrington's argument for teacher ownership and reframing the Portrait itself as "pointillism, not paint-by-number," the product of thousands of small daily interactions rather than a constraining checklist. A practical section walks teachers through using Claude Code in plain language to rebuild tedious Canvas learning-management pages, an Edutopia video section addresses teachers' own shortened attention spans alongside students', and the newsletter closes on historian William Cronon's essay "Only Connect," using his definition of a liberal education as the power to see connections to reframe the entire Portrait initiative: the individual competency "dots" were never the point, the connecting between them was. Taken together, the issue functions as substantive editorial curation rather than a bare link list, using each section's commentary to advance a coherent argument about what the school's new graduate framework actually means in practice.
points: The newsletter directly addresses documented faculty resistance to the new Portrait of a Graduate framework rather than ignoring it, reframing the concern from constraint to liberation via the specific metaphor of 'pointillism, and not paint-by-number.'

Citing Tom Sherrington's argument that sustaining a teaching career requires ownership, 'you need to enjoy it, own it and do the things you want to do,' the CTL uses an outside voice to make the case for teacher agency within a top-down competency framework, rather than simply mandating compliance.

The practical Canvas/Claude Code section models a specific low-barrier AI use case for teachers, rebuilding a tedious learning-management page 'using plain human language,' distinct from more ambitious classroom-AI initiatives, aimed at reclaiming administrative time rather than instruction itself.

The closing citation of Cronon's 'Only Connect' essay does real interpretive work rather than serving as decoration: it retroactively reframes the entire issue's Portrait discussion, arguing the individual competency 'dots' were never the point of a liberal education, the connecting between them was.
quotes: In it Sherrington calls for the importance of teacher ownership writing, in order to sustain a career in teaching, you need to enjoy it, own it and do the things you want to do.

And while that initial response was understandable to a degree, we find real liberation when we view the act of creating a graduate's portrait through a lens of pointillism, and not paint-by-number. In reality one's portrait is a byproduct of thousands of interactions throughout their EA experience, both formal and informal.

Canvas can be a pain to navigate. It's not necessarily difficult. But it is often unnecessarily tedious. Which is why CTL has developed this process to help you build, manipulate, refine, or refresh your Canvas pages using plain human language: no more clicking, no more scrolling, no more frustration.
Many of us are guilty of the very thing we lament in our students, especially in the early days of the school year: that being a short attention span.
He writes: More than anything else, being an educated person means being able to see connections that allow one to make sense of the world and act within it in creative ways.
If our Portrait is the accumulation of thousands of small dots, Cronon reminds us the point was never the dots themselves, but the connecting.
